clue.text: Some reached a café, back or front

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the following words are wanted, a run lying inside them
going back means the hidden run is read from right to left

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the end of reached and the a café that follows

explanation.surface: Someone got to a café and is unsure whether they arrived at its rear or its front entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'reached a café' backwards and FACADE sits inside it; the accent on café is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A facade is the face of a building, the side presented to the street.

clue.text: Lover embraces wife, a timid little creature

indicators.note: to embrace is to wrap your arms around, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: a lover of something is a fan of it
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: An admirer hugs his wife, who is described as a shy little thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the wife the timid creature; in fact the whole phrase defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fawn is a young deer, a small and notoriously skittish animal.

clue.text: Criminal changed course, we're told; that's touching

definitions.note: the phrase 'that's touching' means the thing that is touching, a noun

indicators.note: something we are told is heard rather than read, so it is the spoken sound that counts

blocks.note: a con is a convict, a criminal
a sailing boat that changes course tacks

explanation.surface: A villain alters his route, and someone finds the story moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' pretends to mean emotionally moving; here it means physical contact.
explanation.definitionFit: Contact is the state of physically touching, as two wires in contact.

clue.text: Supply extremely durable uniform

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are used

blocks.note: first and last letters of durable
livery is the distinctive uniform of servants or staff

explanation.surface: A procurement brief asks for very hard-wearing work uniforms.
explanation.definitionFit: A delivery is a supply of goods brought to someone, as a delivery of coal.

clue.text: Ruined – by whisky?

blocks.note: first meaning: put an end to, as a plan or rumour is quashed
second meaning, playful: affected by Scotch whisky, made into a past participle

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is invented for the joke: someone ruined by drink has been done in by Scotch.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a plan is to thwart or ruin it; the whimsical second reading treats Scotch whisky as a verb.

clue.text: Where one shifts stuff from the estate?

definitions.text: Where one shifts stuff from the estate?

blocks.clueFragment: Where one shifts stuff from the estate?
blocks.note: surface reading: the place where unwanted possessions of a country estate or deceased person's estate are cleared

blocks.clueFragment: Where one shifts stuff from the estate?
blocks.note: setter's reading: an estate is a large car, and people sell goods from the back of their cars at this British market

explanation.walkthrough: An estate car is the British term for a station wagon; a car boot sale is a gathering where people sell second-hand goods from their car boots (trunks).
explanation.definitionFit: At such a sale people shift, meaning sell off, their unwanted stuff from the rear of their vehicles.

clue.text: These are up for approval!

blocks.note: surface reading: proposals or candidates put forward to be approved
setter's reading: digits literally raised upward as a gesture that means yes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up for approval' reads like items under review; it is the gesture of raising them.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving a thumbs-up, with both digits raised, is the familiar hand signal of approval.

clue.text: Don't drop anything in bag

blocks.note: first meaning: an instruction to keep a grip on everything, split as two words
second meaning: a large travelling bag

explanation.surface: Someone is warned not to let anything fall out of a bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A holdall is a roomy soft travelling bag, so named because it takes everything.

clue.text: Single-minded cadet died in explosion

indicators.note: an explosion blows things apart, so these letters are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A determined young officer trainee was killed in a blast.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone dedicated is wholly committed to one purpose, which is what single-minded describes.

clue.text: Craftily obtain fish by weight

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for weight
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: Getting hold of fish sold by weight through some sly dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' sets the weight beside the fish, and the weight comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To wangle something is to get it by scheming or trickery.

clue.text: Worried, being stupidly bold? True

indicators.note: acting stupidly means doing things wrongly, so these letters fall out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether anxiety comes from foolish overconfidence, and agrees that it does.
explanation.definitionFit: Troubled and worried are synonyms describing a mind disturbed by anxiety.

clue.text: In Vulcan's gob, an amazing drink

indicators.note: something amazing leaves one bewildered, so these letters are jumbled up

blocks.note: taken as written
the setter's name, apostrophe dropped
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter, Vulcan, raves about a wonderful drink in his mouth; gob is British slang for mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauvignon blanc is a white wine grape and the dry wine made from it, so a drink.

clue.text: Disturbance of ocean may make gulls wonder

indicators.note: to make something from materials is to build it, so these letters are reshaped into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Seabirds might be puzzled by a rough sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundswell is a deep rolling swell of the sea, often caused by a distant storm.

clue.text: Non-stop talker on car journey?

blocks.note: surface reading: a chatterbox passenger who never stops talking during a drive
setter's reading: the slang term for such a talker is a car word joined to the word for the organ of speech

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the car is a playful hint at the first half of the slang word, motor.
explanation.definitionFit: A motormouth is informal for a person who talks incessantly, as if driven by an engine.

clue.text: A way to get goods in proper condition under protective cover

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing placed under another is written below it, so the piece before this word goes second

blocks.note: chain mail is protective armour
things in proper condition are in good order

explanation.surface: Goods arriving in good shape because they were well wrapped in packaging.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'under' puts the condition beneath the cover, so the cover comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Mail order is buying goods from a catalogue and having them posted, a method of shopping.

clue.text: Excess muscle trimmed

indicators.note: something trimmed has had its end cut off, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the gluteus muscles of the buttock are informally glutes

explanation.surface: Too much muscle bulk that a bodybuilder has cut back.
explanation.definitionFit: A glut is an oversupply, more of something than is needed.

clue.text: One may be burning to start attacking the enemy

blocks.note: first meaning: a fire in an unenclosed hearth
second meaning: the military order to begin shooting

explanation.surface: Someone eager to go into battle is described as burning to begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'burning to start' reads as one phrase meaning eager; the break falls after 'burning'.
explanation.definitionFit: An open fire is a hearth blaze in a room; to open fire is to begin shooting.

clue.text: Steal half this short distance

blocks.note: surface reading: take away half of a small span
setter's reading: Cockney rhyming slang for steal is the word half followed by the small unit of length being defined

explanation.walkthrough: Half-inch is Cockney rhyming slang for pinch, i.e. steal; so 'steal' is 'half' plus this distance, an inch.
explanation.definitionFit: An inch is an imperial unit of length, a little over two and a half centimetres, so a short distance.

clue.text: One will change?

blocks.note: surface reading: a person who is going to alter something
setter's reading: a document making an amendment to a last will and testament

explanation.walkthrough: 'will' reads as the future auxiliary; it is the legal document, and 'One will change' means a single alteration to a will.
explanation.definitionFit: A codicil is a supplement to a testament that adds to or alters its provisions.

clue.text: Not obstructed, but having picnic stolen?

blocks.note: first meaning: free to move without hindrance
second meaning, playful: relieved of one's picnic basket, a hamper

explanation.surface: A day out where nothing got in the way, except that the food was taken.
explanation.walkthrough: A hamper is a wicker picnic basket, so losing it leaves you un-hampered.
explanation.definitionFit: Unhampered means free of hindrance; to hamper is to obstruct.

clue.text: Completely destroy way of escape, by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by sound means the words are matched by how they are pronounced, not spelt

blocks.note: a route out is a way of escaping

explanation.surface: An escape path that sounds like it will wipe something out.
explanation.walkthrough: This works for speakers who say route to rhyme with root, as most British speakers do.
explanation.definitionFit: To root out is to eradicate entirely, as weeds are pulled up by the roots.

clue.text: Class out of bed to prepare for parade

blocks.note: a form is a school class in Britain
someone out of bed is up

explanation.surface: A school class is roused early to get ready for a parade.
explanation.definitionFit: To form up is the drill command for troops to get into ranks, ready to parade.

clue.text: You're blind, so no fantastic get-together

indicators.note: something fantastic is fanciful and unreal, so these letters are turned into a fanciful new order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is told they cannot see, so there will be no great party.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy is a former pupil of a British school, and such schools hold gatherings for them.
explanation.definitionFit: An old boys' reunion is a social gathering of former pupils, so a get-together.

clue.text: Unprofitable land, space that's taken up

indicators.note: in a down clue, something taken up is lifted from bottom to top, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: room means space, as in room to move

explanation.surface: Barren ground where all the available room is already occupied.
explanation.definitionFit: A moor is open uncultivated upland, poor ground that yields little for farming.

clue.text: Area of ship shortly burning coal as winter starts

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for the time of year, standing in for the month name

indicators.note: said shortly means cut short, so the last letter is removed

blocks.note: a deck is a floor area of a ship
an ember is a glowing piece of coal

explanation.surface: A ship's deck has coals burning in a brazier as the cold season arrives.
explanation.definitionFit: In the northern hemisphere winter begins in the twelfth month, around the solstice on the 21st.

clue.text: A piece of silk I monopolise for garment

indicators.note: a piece is only part of the whole, so the answer is a run inside the following words

blocks.note: a run of letters across the end of silk, the I, and the start of monopolise

explanation.surface: Someone hogs a length of silk to make clothing from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A kimono is a long, wide-sleeved Japanese robe, a garment often made of silk.

clue.text: Sweet Roland informally at old college

blocks.note: Roly is a pet form of the name Roland
a poly was a polytechnic, a British college type abolished in 1992

explanation.surface: Describes a man named Roland, nicknamed affectionately, when he was a student.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' pretends to describe Roland; it is the British word for a dessert. Roly-poly is a rolled suet pudding with jam.
explanation.definitionFit: Roly-poly pudding is a classic British dessert, and sweet is British for pudding course.

clue.text: Criminal three packing a gun once in America

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so these letters are bent out of their order
packing a thing means holding it inside, so one piece is put within the other

blocks.note: the letters of three rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Three gangsters are carrying a gun, as in an old American crime film; packing is slang for armed.
explanation.definitionFit: Heater was dated US slang for a handgun, common in 1930s gangster talk.
